nodes.name: Unified product multiplication (introduction)
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{inmultireau00} (h_{1}, s_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, s_{2}) := \Bigl( \, h_{1} (s_{1} \triangleright h_{2}) f(s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}, s_{2}), \,\, (s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}) \ast s_{2} \Bigl )
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication on $H\times S$ built from $\triangleright$, $\triangleleft$, $f$, $\ast$.
nodes.label: eq:inmultireau00

nodes.name: Extending structures problem (ES-problem)
nodes.statement: \textbf{(Gr) Extending structures problem.} \textit{Let $H$ be a group and $E$ a set such that $H \subseteq E$. Describe and classify up to an isomorphism that stabilizes $H$ the set of all group structures $\cdot$ that can be defined on $E$ such that $H$ is a subgroup of $(E, \cdot)$.}
nodes.statement_short: Describe and classify, up to isomorphism stabilizing $H$, all group structures on a set $E\supseteq H$ making $H$ a subgroup.

nodes.name: Extension problem of Hölder
nodes.statement: Consider two groups $H$ and $G$. The extension problem of H\"{o}lder consists of describing and classifying all groups $E$ containing $H$ as a normal subgroup such that $E/H \cong G$.
nodes.statement_short: Classify all groups $E$ with normal subgroup $H$ and quotient $E/H\cong G$.

nodes.name: Factorization problem of Ore
nodes.statement: The factorization problem is a "dual" of the extension problem and it was formulated by Ore \cite{Ore}. It consists of describing and classifying up to an isomorphism all groups $E$ that factorize through $H$ and $G$: i.e. $E$ contains $H$ and $G$ as subgroups such that $E = H G$ and $ H \cap G = \{1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Classify all groups $E$ that factorize as $E=HG$ with $H\cap G=\{1\}$.

nodes.name: Factorization problem for two finite cyclic groups
nodes.statement: If $H$ and $G$ are both finite cyclic groups the problem seems to be still open, even though J. Douglas \cite{Douglas} has devoted four papers to the subject.

nodes.name: Pointed set
nodes.statement: Let $(S, 1_S)$ be a pointed set, i.e. $S$ is a non-empty set and $1_S \in S$ is a fixed element in $S$.
differentia: $1_S \in S$ is a fixed element in $S$

nodes.name: Unit notation $1_H$
nodes.statement: The group structures on a set $H$ will be denoted using multiplicative notation and the unit element will be denoted by $1_H$ or only $1$ when there is no danger of confusion.

nodes.name: Notation Aut(H) and |S|
nodes.statement: ${\rm Aut}\, (H)$ denotes the group of automorphisms of a group $H$ and $|S|$ the cardinal of a set $S$.

nodes.name: Unitary map
nodes.statement: A map $r: S \to H$ is called unitary if $r(1_S) = 1_H$.

nodes.name: Right H-set
nodes.statement: $S$ is called a right $H$-set if there exists a right action $\triangleleft : S \times H \rightarrow S$ of $H$ on $S$, i.e. \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ES1} s \triangleleft (h_1 h_2) = (s\triangleleft {h_1} )\triangleleft h_2 \quad \text{and} \quad s \triangleleft {1_H}= s \end{equation} for all $s\in S$, $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$.
nodes.statement_short: $S$ is a right $H$-set if it carries a right action $\triangleleft$ of $H$.

nodes.name: Right action axioms
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{ES1} s \triangleleft (h_1 h_2) = (s\triangleleft {h_1} )\triangleleft h_2 \quad \text{and} \quad s \triangleleft {1_H}= s
nodes.label: eq:ES1

nodes.name: Trivial action
nodes.statement: The action $\triangleleft : S \times H \rightarrow S$ is called the trivial action if $s \triangleleft h = s$, for all $s\in S$ and $h\in H$.

nodes.name: Trivial maps
nodes.statement: Similarly the maps $ \triangleright : S \times H \to H$ and $f: S \times S \to H$ are called trivial maps if $ s \triangleright h = h$ and respectively $f (s_1, s_2) = 1_H$, for all $s$, $s_1$, $s_2 \in S$ and $h\in H$.

nodes.name: Notation for a map into Aut(H)
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a group and $\alpha : G \rightarrow {\rm Aut}\, (H)$ is a map we use the similar notation $ \alpha (g) (h) = g\triangleright h$, for all $g\in G$ and $h\in H$.

nodes.name: Crossed system of groups
nodes.statement: A \textit{crossed system} of groups is a quadruple $(H, G, \alpha, f)$, where $H$ and $G$ are two groups, $\alpha : G \rightarrow {\rm Aut}\, (H)$ and $f : G \times G \rightarrow H$ are two maps such that the following compatibility conditions hold: \begin{eqnarray} g_1 \triangleright (g_2\triangleright h) &=& f(g_1, g_2) \, \bigl((g_1g_2)\triangleright h \bigl)\, f(g_1, g_2)^{-1} \eqlabel{WA} \\ f(g_1,\, g_2)\, f(g_1 g_2, \, g_3) &=& \bigl(g_1 \triangleright f(g_2, \, g_3) \bigl) \, f(g_1, \, g_2g_3) \eqlabel{CC} \end{eqnarray} for all $g_1$, $g_2$, $g_3 \in G$ and $h\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: A quadruple $(H,G,\alpha,f)$ satisfying the twisted-action and cocycle conditions.

nodes.name: Crossed system compatibility conditions (WA), (CC)
nodes.statement: g_1 \triangleright (g_2\triangleright h) &=& f(g_1, g_2) \, \bigl((g_1g_2)\triangleright h \bigl)\, f(g_1, g_2)^{-1} \eqlabel{WA} \\ f(g_1,\, g_2)\, f(g_1 g_2, \, g_3) &=& \bigl(g_1 \triangleright f(g_2, \, g_3) \bigl) \, f(g_1, \, g_2g_3) \eqlabel{CC}
nodes.label: eq:WA

nodes.name: Normalized crossed system
nodes.statement: The crossed system $\Gamma = (H, G, \alpha, f)$ is called \textit{normalized} if $f(1, 1) = 1$.

nodes.name: Weak action and alpha-cocycle
nodes.statement: The map $\alpha : G \rightarrow {\rm Aut}\, (H)$ is called a \textit{weak action} and $f : G \times G \rightarrow H$ is called an $\alpha$-\textit{cocycle}.

nodes.name: Crossed product multiplication on H x G
nodes.statement: Let $H \#_{\alpha}^{f} \, G : = H\times G$ as a set with a binary operation defined by the formula: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{41} (h_1,\, g_1)\cdot (h_2, \, g_2) : = \bigl( h_1 (g_1 \triangleright h_2) f(g_1, \, g_2), \, g_1g_2 \bigl) \end{equation} for all $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$, $g_1$, $g_2 \in G$.

nodes.name: Crossed product multiplication
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{41} (h_1,\, g_1)\cdot (h_2, \, g_2) : = \bigl( h_1 (g_1 \triangleright h_2) f(g_1, \, g_2), \, g_1g_2 \bigl)
nodes.label: eq:41

nodes.name: Associativity criterion for crossed products
nodes.statement: It is well known that the multiplication on $H \#_{\alpha}^{f} \, G$ given by (\ref{eq:41}) is associative if and only if $(H, G, \alpha, f)$ is a crossed system (see for instance \cite[Theorem 2.3]{am1}).
conclusions: the multiplication on $H \#_{\alpha}^{f} \, G$ given by (\ref{eq:41}) is associative if and only if $(H, G, \alpha, f)$ is a crossed system

nodes.name: Crossed product of groups
nodes.statement: In this case $\bigl ( H \#_{\alpha}^{f} \, G, \, \cdot \bigl)$ is a group with unit $1_{H \#_{\alpha}^{f} \, G} = \bigl( f(1, 1) ^{-1}, \, 1\bigl)$ called the \textit{crossed product of $H$ and $G$} associated to the crossed system $(H, G, \alpha, f)$.

nodes.name: Semidirect product
nodes.statement: A crossed product with $f$ the trivial cocycle (that is $f(g_1, \, g_2) = 1_H$, for all $g_1$, $g_2 \in G$) is just $H \ltimes_{\alpha} G$, the semidirect product of $H$ and $G$.

nodes.name: Schreier's theorem
nodes.statement: \relabel{recon} Schreier's theorem states that any extension $E$ of $H$ by a group $G$ is equivalent to a crossed product extension. We recall in detail this construction for further use. Let $H\unlhd E$ be a normal subgroup of a group $E$ and $G := E/H$ the quotient group. Let $\pi : E \to G$ be the canonical projection and $\chi : G \to E$ be a section as a map of $\pi$ with $\chi (1_G) = 1_E$. Using $\chi$ we define a weak action $\alpha$ and a cocycle $f$ by the formulas: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{1act} \alpha : G \rightarrow {\rm Aut}\, (H), \qquad \, \alpha (g) (h) = g \triangleright h : = \chi (g) h \chi (g)^{-1} \end{equation} \begin{equation}\eqlabel{1coc} f : G \times G \rightarrow H, \qquad f (g_1, g_2) := \chi (g_1) \chi (g_2) \chi (g_1 g_2)^{-1} \end{equation} for all $g\in G$, $g_1$, $g_2 \in G$ and $h\in H$. Then $(H, G, \alpha, f)$ is a normalized crossed system of groups and $$ \theta : H \#_{\alpha}^{f} \, G \to E, \qquad \theta (h, g) := h \chi (g) $$ is an isomorphism of groups. For more details we refer the reader to \cite[Theorem 2.6]{am1}.
nodes.statement_short: Every extension of $H$ by $G=E/H$ is a crossed product $H\#_\alpha^f G$ built from a section $\chi$ of $E\to G$.
assumptions: Let $H\unlhd E$ be a normal subgroup of a group $E$ and $G := E/H$ the quotient group.
conclusions: Then $(H, G, \alpha, f)$ is a normalized crossed system of groups
nodes.label: re:recon

nodes.name: Weak action from a section
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{1act} \alpha : G \rightarrow {\rm Aut}\, (H), \qquad \, \alpha (g) (h) = g \triangleright h : = \chi (g) h \chi (g)^{-1}
nodes.label: eq:1act

nodes.name: Cocycle from a section
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{1coc} f : G \times G \rightarrow H, \qquad f (g_1, g_2) := \chi (g_1) \chi (g_2) \chi (g_1 g_2)^{-1}
nodes.label: eq:1coc

nodes.name: Matched pair of groups
nodes.statement: A \textit{matched pair} of groups is a quadruple $ (H, G, \triangleright, \triangleleft) $, where $\triangleright: G \times H \rightarrow H$ is a left action of the group $G$ on the set $H$, $\triangleleft : G \times H \rightarrow G$ is a right action of the group $H$ on the set $G$ such that: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{2} g \triangleright (h_{1} h_{2}) = (g \triangleright h_{1})\bigl((g \triangleleft h_{1}) \triangleright h_{2}\bigl) \end{equation} \begin{equation}\eqlabel{3} (g_{1} g_{2}) \triangleleft h = \bigl(g_{1} \triangleleft (g_{2} \triangleright h)\bigl)(g_{2} \triangleleft h) \end{equation} for all $h$, $h_{1}$, $h_{2} \in H$ and $g$, $g_{1}$, $g_{2} \in G$ (see \cite{Takeuchi}).
nodes.statement_short: Two mutual actions $\triangleright$, $\triangleleft$ between groups $H$, $G$ satisfying two compatibility conditions.

nodes.name: Matched pair condition (2)
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{2} g \triangleright (h_{1} h_{2}) = (g \triangleright h_{1})\bigl((g \triangleleft h_{1}) \triangleright h_{2}\bigl)
nodes.label: eq:2

nodes.name: Matched pair condition (3)
nodes.statement: \eqlabel{3} (g_{1} g_{2}) \triangleleft h = \bigl(g_{1} \triangleleft (g_{2} \triangleright h)\bigl)(g_{2} \triangleleft h)
nodes.label: eq:3

nodes.name: Bicrossed product multiplication on H x G
nodes.statement: Let $H \bowtie \, G : = H\times G$ as a set with a binary operation defined by the formula: \begin{equation} (h_{1}, g_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, g_{2}) = \bigl( h_{1}(g_{1} \triangleright h_{2}), \, (g_{1} \triangleleft h_{2})g_{2}\bigl) \end{equation} for all $h_{1}$, $h_{2} \in H$ and $g_{1}$, $g_{2} \in G$.

nodes.name: Bicrossed product multiplication
nodes.statement: (h_{1}, g_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, g_{2}) = \bigl( h_{1}(g_{1} \triangleright h_{2}), \, (g_{1} \triangleleft h_{2})g_{2}\bigl)

nodes.name: Bicrossed product is a group iff matched pair
nodes.statement: It can be easily shown that $H \bowtie \, G $ is a group with $(1_{H}, 1_{G})$ as a unit if and only if $(H, G, \triangleright, \triangleleft)$ is a matched pair of groups.
conclusions: $H \bowtie \, G $ is a group with $(1_{H}, 1_{G})$ as a unit if and only if $(H, G, \triangleright, \triangleleft)$ is a matched pair of groups

nodes.name: Bicrossed product (knit / Zappa-Szep product)
nodes.statement: In this case $H \bowtie \, G $ is called the \textit{bicrossed product, doublecross product, knit product or Zappa-Szep product} associated to the matched pair $(H, G, \triangleright, \triangleleft)$.

nodes.name: Takeuchi's theorem
nodes.statement: Takeuchi proved \cite{Takeuchi} that a group $E$ factorizes through two subgroups $H$ and $G$ if and only if $E$ is isomorphic to a bicrossed product $H \bowtie \, G$ associated to a matched pair $(H, G, \triangleright, \triangleleft)$.
conclusions: a group $E$ factorizes through two subgroups $H$ and $G$ if and only if $E$ is isomorphic to a bicrossed product $H \bowtie \, G$

nodes.name: Reconstruction theorem from a subgroup
nodes.statement: \thlabel{splitrec} Let $H \leq E$ be a subgroup of a group $E$. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a map $p : E \to H$ such that $p (1) = 1$ and for any $h\in H$, $x\in E$ \begin{equation}\eqlabel{33ab} p ( h \, x ) = h \, p (x) \end{equation} \item For such a map $p : E \to H$ we define $S = S_p := p^{-1}(1) = \{ x\in E \, |\, p (x) = 1 \}$. Then the multiplication map \begin{equation}\eqlabel{335b} \varphi : H \times S \to E, \quad \varphi ( h, s) := h s \end{equation} for all $h\in H$ and $s\in S$ is bijective with the inverse given for any $x\in E$ by $$ \varphi^{-1} : E \to H \times S, \quad \varphi^{-1} (x) = \bigl( p(x), \, p (x)^{-1} \, x \bigl) $$ \item For $p$ and $S$ as above there exist four maps $ \triangleright = \triangleright_p: S\times H \to H$, $\triangleleft = \triangleleft_p : S\times H \to S$, $f = f_p : S\times S \to H$ and $\ast = \ast_p : S\times S \to S$ given by the formulas \begin{eqnarray*} s \triangleright h &{:=}& p (sh), \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, s\triangleleft h := p(sh)^{-1} s h \eqlabel{acti12}\\ f(s_1, s_2) &{:=}& p (s_1 s_2), \,\,\,\, s_1 \ast s_2 := p(s_1 s_2)^{-1} s_1 s_2 \end{eqnarray*} for all $s$, $s_1$, $s_2 \in S$ and $h\in H$. Using these maps, the unique group structure $'\cdot'$ on the set $H \times S$ such that $\varphi : (H \times S, \cdot) \to E$ is an isomorphism of groups is given by: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{inmultireau} (h_{1}, s_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, s_{2}) := \Bigl( \, h_{1} (s_{1} \triangleright h_{2}) f(s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}, s_{2}), \,\, (s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}) \ast s_{2} \Bigl ) \end{equation} for all $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2\in S$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: (1) Using the axiom of choice we can fix $ \Gamma = (x_i)_{i\in I} \subset E $ to be a system of representatives for the right congruence modulo $H$ in $E$ such that $1 \in \Gamma$. Then for any $x\in E$ there exists an unique $h_x \in H$ and an unique $x_{i_0} \in \Gamma$ such that $x = h_x \, x_{i_0}$. Thus, there exists a well defined map $p : E \to H$ given by the formula $p (x) := h_x$, for all $x\in E$. As $1 \in \Gamma$ we have that $ p (1) = 1$. Moreover, for any $h\in H$ and $x\in E$ we have that $h x = h h_x \, x_{i_0}$. Thus $p (h x) = h h_x = h p(x)$, as needed. (2) We note that $p (x)^{-1} x \in S$ as $ p \bigl( p (x)^{-1} \, x \bigl) = p (x)^{-1} p(x) = 1 $, for all $x\in E$. The rest is straightforward. (3) First we note that $\triangleleft$ and $\ast$ are well defined maps. Next, we can easily prove that the following two formulas hold: \begin{eqnarray} p(s_1 h_2 s_2) &=& (s_1 \triangleright h_2) f (s_1 \triangleleft h_2 , s_2) \eqlabel{inmaa} \\ (s_1 \triangleleft h_2) \ast s_2 &=& p (s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2 \eqlabel{inmab} \end{eqnarray} for all $s_1$, $s_2\in S$ and $h_2 \in H$. Indeed, \begin{eqnarray*} (s_1 \triangleright h_2) f (s_1 \triangleleft h_2 , s_2) &{=}& p(s_1 h_2) \, p\bigl( (s_1 \triangleleft h_2) s_2 \bigl)\\ &{=}& p(s_1 h_2) \, p \bigl( p(s_1 h_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2 \bigl)\\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:33ab})} {=}& p (s_1 h_2 s_2) \end{eqnarray*} Similarly, we can prove that (\ref{eq:inmab}) holds. Now, $\varphi : H \times S \to E$ is a bijection between the set $H \times S$ and the group $E$. Thus, there exists a unique group structure $\cdot$ on the set $H \times S$ such that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of groups. This group structure is obtained by transferring the group structure from $E$ via the bijection $\varphi$, i.e. is given by: \begin{eqnarray*} (h_{1}, s_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, s_{2}) &{=}& \varphi^{-1} \bigl( \varphi (h_1, s_1) \varphi (h_2, s_2) \bigl) \,\, = \varphi^{-1} (h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2)\\ &{=}& \bigl( p(h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2), \, p(h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2 \bigl)\\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:33ab})} {=}& \bigl( h_1 p(s_1 h_2 s_2), \, p(s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2\bigl) \\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:inmaa}), (\ref{eq:inmab})} {=}& \Bigl( \, h_{1} (s_{1} \triangleright h_{2}) f(s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}, \, s_{2}), \,\, (s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}) \ast s_{2} \Bigl ) \end{eqnarray*} for all $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2\in S$ as needed.
nodes.section: 2 Group extending structures and unified products
nodes.statement_short: Construct $p$ from a system of right coset representatives (axiom of choice); then transport the group structure of $E$ along the bijection $\varphi$.

nodes.name: Normalizing conditions and twisted associativity of the maps from p
nodes.statement: \relabel{cecon} As $1\in S$ and $p(s) = 1$, for all $s\in S$ the maps $ \triangleright = \triangleright_p$, $\triangleleft = \triangleleft_p$, $f = f_p $ and $\ast = \ast_p$ constructed in (3) of Theorem~\ref{th:splitrec} satisfy the following normalizing conditions: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{nor1} s \triangleright 1 = 1, \quad 1 \triangleright h = h, \quad 1 \triangleleft h = 1, \quad s\triangleleft 1 = s \end{equation} \begin{equation}\eqlabel{nor2} f(s, 1) = f(1, s) = 1, \quad s\ast 1 = 1 \ast s = s \end{equation} for all $s\in S$ and $h\in H$. Hence, the multiplication $\ast$ on $S$ has a unit but is not necessary associative. In fact, we can easily prove that it satisfies the following compatibility: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ES7ab} (s_{1} \ast s_{2}) \ast s_{3} = \bigl( s_{1} \triangleleft f(s_{2},s_{3}) \bigl ) \ast (s_{2} \ast s_{3}) \end{equation} for all $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3 \in S$, i.e. $\ast$ is associative up to the pair $(\triangleleft, f)$. Moreover, any element $s\in S$ is left invertible in $(S, \ast)$; more precisely we can show that for any $s\in S$ there exists a unique element $s' \in S$ such that $s' \ast s = 1$.

nodes.name: Extending datum of a group
nodes.statement: \delabel{hgroup} Let $H$ be a group. An \textit{extending datum of $H$} is a system $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ where: $(1)$ $(S, 1_S)$ is a pointed set, $\ast: S \times S \to S$ is a binary operation such that for any $s\in S$ \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ES3} s\ast 1_S = 1_S \ast s = s \end{equation} $(2)$ The maps $\triangleleft : S\times H \to S$, $\triangleright: S\times H \to H$ and $f : S\times S \to H$ satisfy the following normalizing conditions for any $s\in S$ and $h\in H$: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{nor1a} s\triangleleft 1_H = s, \,\, 1_S \triangleleft h = 1_S, \,\, 1_S \triangleright h = h, \,\, s\triangleright 1_H = 1_H, \,\, f(s, 1_S) = f(1_S, s) = 1_H \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: A pointed set with unital operation $\ast$ and normalized maps $\triangleleft$, $\triangleright$, $f$.

nodes.name: The product H ⋉ S of an extending datum
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a group and $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ an extending datum of $H$. We denote by $H \ltimes_{\Omega(H)} S$ := $H \ltimes S$ the set $H\times S$ with the binary operation defined by the formula: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{13a} (h_{1}, s_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, s_{2}) := \Bigl( \, h_{1} (s_{1} \triangleright h_{2}) f(s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}, s_{2}), \,\, (s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}) \ast s_{2} \Bigl ) \end{equation} for all $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2\in S$.

nodes.name: Unified product; group extending structure
nodes.statement: \delabel{unifprod} Let $H$ be a group and $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ an extending datum of $H$. The object $H \ltimes S$ introduced above is called \textit{the unified product of $H$ and $\Omega(H)$} if $H \ltimes S$ is a group with the multiplication given by (\ref{eq:13a}). In this case the extending datum $\Omega(H)$ is called a \textit{group extending structure} of $H$. The maps $\triangleright$ and $\triangleleft$ are called the \textit{actions} of $\Omega(H)$ and $f$ is called the $(\triangleright, \triangleleft)$-\textit{cocycle} of $\Omega(H)$.

nodes.name: Axioms for a unified product (ES1)-(ES7)
nodes.statement: \thlabel{constr} Let $H$ be a group and $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ an extending datum of $H$. The following statements are equivalent: $(1)$ $A \ltimes H$ is an unified product; $(2)$ The following compatibilities hold for any $s$, $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3 \in S$ and $h$, $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$: \begin{enumerate} \item[(ES1)] The map $\triangleleft : S\times H \to S$ is a right action of the group $H$ on the set $S$; \item[(ES2)] $(s_{1} \ast s_{2}) \ast s_{3} = \bigl( s_{1} \triangleleft f(s_{2},s_{3}) \bigl ) \ast (s_{2} \ast s_{3});$ \item[(ES3)] $s \triangleright(h_{1} h_{2}) = (s \triangleright h_{1}) \bigl( (s \triangleleft h_{1}) \triangleright h_{2} \bigl);$ \item[(ES4)] $(s_{1} \ast s_{2}) \triangleleft h = \bigl ( s_{1} \triangleleft (s_{2} \triangleright h) \bigl ) \ast (s_{2} \triangleleft h);$ \item[(ES5)] $\bigl( s_{1} \triangleright(s_{2}\triangleright h)\bigl) f \bigl( s_{1} \triangleleft (s_{2}\triangleright h), \, s_{2} \triangleleft h \bigl ) = f(s_{1}, \, s_{2}) \bigl( (s_{1} \ast s_{2} ) \triangleright h \bigl);$ \item[(ES6)] $f(s_{1}, \, s_{2}) f(s_{1} \ast s_{2}, \, s_{3}) = \bigl (s_{1} \triangleright f(s_{2}, \, s_{3})\bigl ) f\bigl (s_{1} \triangleleft f(s_{2}, s_{3}), \, s_{2} \ast s_{3}\bigl );$ \item[(ES7)] For any $s\in S$ there exists $s'\in S$ such that $s' \ast s = 1_S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: $H\ltimes S$ is a group iff the extending datum satisfies the seven compatibilities (ES1)-(ES7).

nodes.name: ES axioms versus matched-pair and crossed-system conditions
nodes.statement: Before going into the proof of the theorem we note that $(ES3)$ and $(ES4)$ are exactly, mutatis-mutandis, the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:2}) and (\ref{eq:3}) from the definition of a matched pair of groups while $(ES5)$ and $(ES6)$ are deformations via the right action $\triangleleft$ of the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:WA}) and (\ref{eq:CC}) from the definition of a crossed system of groups. The axiom $(ES1)$ is called the \emph{twisted associativity condition} as it measures how far $\ast$ is from being associative, i.e. from being a group structure on $S$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: (ES3),(ES4) are the matched-pair conditions; (ES5),(ES6) deform the crossed-system conditions; the associativity axiom is the twisted associativity condition.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.5
nodes.statement: We know that $(1_{H}, 1_{S})$ is a unit for the operation defined by (\ref{eq:13a}). We prove now that $\cdot$ given by (\ref{eq:13a}) is associative if and only if the compatibility conditions $(ES1) - (ES6)$ hold. Assume first that $\cdot$ is associative and let $h$, $h_{1}$, $h_{2} \in H$ and $s$, $s_1$, $s_{2} \in S$. The associativity condition $$ [(1_H, s)\cdot (h_{1}, 1_S)]\cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (1_H, s)\cdot [(h_{1}, 1_S)\cdot (h_2, 1_S)] $$ gives, after we use the cross relations (\ref{eq:15}) and (\ref{eq:13}), $ (s \triangleright h_1, \, s\triangleleft h_1 ) \cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (1_H, s) \cdot (h_1 h_2, \, 1_S)$. Thus $ \Bigl((s \triangleright h_{1}) \bigl( (s \triangleleft h_{1}) \triangleright h_{2} \bigl), \, (s\triangleleft h_1) \triangleleft h_2 \Bigl) = \bigl(s \triangleright (h_1 h_2), \, s \triangleleft (h_1 h_2) \bigl)$ and hence $(ES1)$ and $(ES3)$ hold. Now, by writing the associativity condition $[(1_H, s_1)\cdot (1_H, s_2)]\cdot (1_H, s_3) = (1_H, s_1)\cdot [(1_H, s_2)\cdot (1_H, s_3)]$ and computing this equality using the cross relation (\ref{eq:14}) it follows that the compatibility conditions $(ES2)$ and $(ES6)$ hold. Finally, if we write the associativity condition $[(1_H, s_1)\cdot (1_H, s_2)]\cdot (h, 1_S) = (1_H, s_1)\cdot [(1_H, s_2)\cdot (h, 1_S)]$ and use (\ref{eq:14}) and then (\ref{eq:15}) we obtain that $(ES4)$ and $(ES5)$ hold. Conversely, assume that the compatibility conditions $(ES1) - (ES6)$ hold. Then, by a rather long but straightforward computation, which can be provided upon request, we can prove that the operation $\cdot$ is associative, that is $(h_{1}, s_{1})\cdot [(h_{2}, s_{2}) \cdot (h_{3}, s_{3})] = [(h_{1}, s_{1})\cdot (h_{2}, s_{2})]\cdot (h_{3}, s_{3})$, for all $h_1$, $h_2$, $h_{3} \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_{3} \in S$. To conclude, we have proved that $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is a monoid if and only if $(ES1) - (ES6)$ hold. Assume now that $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is a monoid: it remains to be proved that the monoid is actually a group if and only if $(ES7)$ holds. Indeed, in the monoid $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ we have: $$ (h, 1_S)\cdot (1_H, s) = (h, s), \qquad (h_1, 1_S) \cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (h_1 h_2, 1_S) $$ for all $h$, $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s\in S$. In particular, any element of the form $(h, 1_S)$, for $h\in H$ is invertible in $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$. Now, a monoid is a group if and only if each of his elements has a left inverse. As $\cdot$ is associative it follows from: $$ (h^{-1}, 1_S)\cdot (h, s) = (1_H, s) $$ that $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is a group if and only if $(1_H, s)$ has a left inverse for all $s\in S$. Hence, for any $s\in S$ there exist elements $s' \in S$ and $h'\in H$ such that $$ (h' , s' ) \cdot (1_H, s) = \bigl ( h' f (s', s), \, s' \ast s\bigl ) = (1_H, 1_S) $$ This is of course equivalent to the fact that $s' \ast s = 1_S$ for all $s \in S$ and $h' = f\bigl( s', \, s \bigl)^{-1}$. The proof is now finished. We note that the inverse of an element $(h, s)$ in the group $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is given by the formula $$ (h, \, s)^{-1} = \bigl( f(s', \, s)^{-1} (s' \triangleright h^{-1}), \, s' \triangleleft h^{-1}\bigl) $$ where $s' \ast s = 1_S$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate associativity on generators $(h,1_S)$, $(1_H,s)$ to get (ES1)-(ES6), and the converse by computation. Then a monoid is a group iff every $(1_H,s)$ has a left inverse, which is (ES7).

nodes.name: Unified product recovers its extending structure via p_H
nodes.statement: \relabel{cumsefac} Let $H$ be a group, $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ a group extending datum of $H$ and $H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$ the associated unified product. Then the canonical inclusion $$ i_H : H \to H \ltimes_{\Omega} S, \qquad i_H (h) := (h, 1_S) $$ is a morphism of groups and the map $$ p_H : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H, \qquad p_H (h, s) := h $$ satisfies condition (\ref{eq:33ab}) of Theorem~\ref{th:splitrec}. Moreover, if we identify $H \cong (H, 1_S) \leq H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$ and $S \cong (1_H, S) \subset H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$ we can easily show that the maps $\ast$, $\triangleleft$, $\triangleright$ and $f$ from the definition of $\Omega(H)$ are exactly the ones given in (3) of Theorem~\ref{th:splitrec} associated to the splitting map $p_H$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: $i_H$ is a group morphism and the projection $p_H$ is $H$-linear and recovers the maps of $\Omega(H)$ via Theorem 2.1.
nodes.label: re:cumsefac

nodes.name: Description of group structures containing H (ES-problem, description part)
nodes.statement: \colabel{primaint} Let $H$ be a group and $E$ a set such that $H \subseteq E$. Then there exists a group structure $\cdot$ on $E$ such that $H$ is a subgroup of $(E, \cdot)$ if and only if there exists a group extending structure $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ of $H$ such that $ H \ltimes S \cong (E, \cdot)$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Group structures on $E$ containing $H$ as subgroup are exactly unified products $H\ltimes S\cong E$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a group and $E$ a set such that $H \subseteq E$.
conclusions: there exists a group structure $\cdot$ on $E$ such that $H$ is a subgroup of $(E, \cdot)$ if and only if there exists a group extending structure

nodes.name: Crossed product as a unified product
nodes.statement: \exlabel{cazpar} Let $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ be an extending datum of $H$ such that $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action, that is $s \triangleleft h := s$, for all $s \in S$ and $h\in H$. Then $\Omega (H) $ is a group extending structure of $H$ if and only if $(S, \ast)$ is a group structure on the set $S$ and $(H, (S, \ast), \triangleright, f)$ is a crossed system of groups. In this case, the associated unified product $H\ltimes_{\Omega} S = H \#_{\triangleright}^{f} \, G $ is the crossed product of groups.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: With trivial $\triangleleft$, group extending structures are crossed systems and the unified product is the crossed product.
nodes.label: ex:cazpar

nodes.name: Bicrossed product as a unified product
nodes.statement: \exlabel{cazparb} Let $\Omega(H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ be an extending datum of $H$ such that $f$ is the trivial cocycle, that is $f(s_1, s_2) = 1$, for all $s_1$, $s_2\in S$. Then $\Omega (H) $ is a group extending structure of $H$ if and only if $(S, \ast)$ is a group structure on the set $S$ and $(H, (S, \ast), \triangleright, \triangleleft)$ is a matched pair of groups. In this case, the associated unified product $A\ltimes_{\Omega} H = H \bowtie \, G $ is the bicrossed product of groups.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: With trivial cocycle $f$, group extending structures are matched pairs and the unified product is the bicrossed product.
nodes.label: ex:cazparb

nodes.name: A6 as a unified product
nodes.statement: There exist examples of groups that cannot be written either as a crossed product or as a bicrossed product of two groups of smaller order. Such a group should be a simple group (otherwise it can be written as a crossed product). The simple group of smallest order that cannot be written as a bicrossed product is the alternating group $A_6$ (\cite{WW}). The above results allows us to write $A_6$, and in fact any other simple group which is not a bicrossed product, as a unified product between one of its subgroups and an extending structure. For instance, we can write $$ A_6 \cong A_4 \ltimes_{\Omega} S $$ for an extending structure $\Omega (A_4) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$, where $S$ is a set with 30 elements.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: $A_6$ is neither a crossed nor a bicrossed product but is $A_4\ltimes_\Omega S$ with $|S|=30$.

nodes.name: Group extending structure from a transition map gamma
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a group, $(S, 1_S, \ast)$ a pointed set with a binary operation $ \ast : S \times S \to S$ having $1_S$ as a unit. Let $ \triangleleft : S \times H \to S$ be a map such that $(S, \triangleleft)$ is a right $H$-set and $\gamma : S \to H$ be a map with $\gamma (1_S) = 1_H$ such that the following compatibilities hold \begin{eqnarray*} (x \ast y) \ast z &=& \Bigl ( x \triangleleft \bigl( \gamma(y) \, \gamma (z) \, \gamma (y\ast z) ^{-1} \bigl) \Bigl ) \, \ast \, (y \ast z) \eqlabel{be1}\\ (x \ast y) \triangleleft g &=& \Bigl( x \triangleleft \bigl( \gamma (y) \, g \, \gamma ( y \triangleleft g )^{-1} \bigl) \Bigl) \, \ast \, (y \triangleleft g) \eqlabel{be3} \end{eqnarray*} for all $g\in H$, $x$, $y$, $z\in S$. Using the transition map $\gamma$ we define a left action $\triangleright$ and a cocycle $f$ via: $$ x \triangleright g := \gamma (x) \, g \,\gamma (x \triangleleft g) ^{-1}, \quad f (x, \, y) := \gamma (x) \, \gamma (y) \, \gamma (x \ast y)^{-1} $$ for all $x$, $y\in S$ and $g\in H$. Then we can prove that $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ is a group extending structure of $H$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: A right $H$-set with unital $\ast$ and a transition map $\gamma$ satisfying two compatibilities yields a group extending structure.

Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S, (i_H, i_S))$ is an initial object of ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$, where $i_H : H\rightarrow H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$ and $i_S:S\rightarrow H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$ are the canonical inclusions; \item[(2)] $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S, (\pi_H, \pi_S))$ is a final object of ${\mathcal D}_{\Omega (H)}$, where $\pi_H : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S\rightarrow H $ and $\pi_S :H \ltimes_{\Omega} S\rightarrow S$ are the canonical projections. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.12
nodes.statement: $(1)$ It is easy to see that $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S, (i_H, i_S))$ is an object in the category ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$. Let $(G, (u,v))$ be an object in ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$. We need to prove that there exists an unique morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \rightarrow G$ such that the following diagram commutes: $$ \xymatrix{ H\ar[r]^{i_{H}}\ar[dr]_{u} & H \ltimes_{\Omega} S\ar[d]^{\psi} & S\ar[l]_{i_{S}}\ar[dl]^{v} \\ &G } $$ Assume first that $\psi$ satisfies the above condition. We obtain: $\psi ((h,s)) = \psi((h, 1_S) \cdot(1_H, s)) = \psi ((h, 1_S)) \psi((1_H, s)) = (\psi \circ i_H)(h) (\psi \circ i_S)(s)) = u(h)v(s)$, for all $h \in H$, $s \in S$ and we proved that $\psi$ is uniquely determined by $u$ and $v$. The existence of $\psi$ can be proved as follows: we define $\psi: H\ltimes_{\Omega} S \rightarrow G$ by $\psi ((h, s)) := u(h)v(s)$, for all $h\in H$ and $s\in S$. The fact that $\psi$ is a morphism of groups is just a straightforward computation and the commutativity of the diagram is obvious. $(2)$ Similar to $(1)$.
nodes.section: The universal properties of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness: any $\psi$ must be $\psi(h,s)=u(h)v(s)$; existence: this formula defines a group morphism. Part (2) is dual.

nodes.statement: Using Corollary~\ref{co:primaint}, the classification of all group structures on $E$ that contain $H$ as a subgroup, reduces to the classification of all unified products $H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$, associated to all group extending structures $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$, for a set $S$ such that $|H| |S| = |E|$.

nodes.name: Morphism stabilizing H (resp. S)
nodes.statement: \delabel{diagdef} Let $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ and $\Omega ' (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_{S}, \ast'), \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f' \bigl)$ be two group extending structures of $H$ and $H \ltimes_{\Omega} S$, $H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ the associated unified products. For a morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ we consider the following diagram \begin{equation}\eqlabel{D2} \xymatrix {& H \ar[r]^{i_{H}} \ar[d]_{Id_{H}} & {H\ltimes S} \ar[r]^{\pi_{S}}\ar[d]^{\psi} & S\ar[d]^{Id_{S}}\\ & H\ar[r]^{i_{H}} & {H\ltimes' S}\ar[r]^{\pi_{S}} & S} \end{equation} where $\pi_S : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to S$ is the canonical projection $\pi (h, s) := s$, for all $h\in H$ and $s\in S$. We say that $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ \emph{stabilizes} $H$ (resp. stabilizes $S$) if the left square (resp. the right square) of the diagram (\ref{eq:D2}) is commutative.

nodes.name: Morphisms of unified products stabilizing H
nodes.statement: \prlabel{clasif1} Let $H$ be a group, $(S, 1_S)$, $(S', 1_{S'})$ two pointed sets and $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ and $\Omega ' (H) = \bigl( (S', 1_{S'}, \ast'), \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f' \bigl)$ be two group extending structures of $H$. Then there exists a bijective correspondence between the set of all morphisms of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S'$ that stabilize $H$ and the set of all pairs $(r, v)$, where $r: S \rightarrow H$, $v: S \rightarrow S'$ are two unitary maps such that: \begin{eqnarray} v(s \triangleleft h) &=& v(s) \triangleleft' h \eqlabel{p1} \\ (s \triangleright h) \, r(s \triangleleft h) &=& r(s)\, \bigl(v(s) \triangleright' h \bigl)\eqlabel{p2} \\ v(s_{1} \ast s_{2}) &=& \bigl( v(s_{1}) \triangleleft' r(s_{2})\bigl) \, \ast' \, v(s_{2}) \eqlabel{p3}\\ f(s_1, s_2) \, r(s_{1} * s_{2}) &=& r(s_{1}) \, \bigl( v(s_{1}) \triangleright' r(s_{2}) \bigl) \, f' \bigl( v(s_{1}) \triangleleft' r(s_{2}), \, v(s_2) \bigl) \eqlabel{p4} \end{eqnarray} for all $s$, $s_{1}$, $s_{2} \in S$ and $h \in H$. Through the above correspondence the morphism $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S'$ corresponding to $(r, v)$ is given by \begin{equation}\eqlabel{p5} \psi(h, \, s) = \bigl(h \, r(s), \, v(s)\bigl) \end{equation} for all $h \in H$, $s \in S$. Furthermore, $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S'$ given by (\ref{eq:p5}) is an isomorphisms of groups if and only if $v: S \to S'$ is bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Group morphisms $H\ltimes_\Omega S\to H\ltimes_{\Omega'}S'$ stabilizing $H$ correspond to unitary pairs $(r,v)$ satisfying (30)-(33); isomorphisms iff $v$ bijective.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a group, $(S, 1_S)$, $(S', 1_{S'})$ two pointed sets
conclusions: there exists a bijective correspondence between the set of all morphisms of groups
is an isomorphisms of groups if and only if $v: S \to S'$ is bijective.
nodes.label: pr:clasif1

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.14
nodes.statement: A morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S'$ that makes the left square of the diagram (\ref{eq:D2}) commutative is uniquely determined by two maps $r = r_{\psi}: S \rightarrow H$, $v = v_{\psi}: S \rightarrow S'$ such that $\psi(1, s) = \bigl( r(s), v(s)\bigl)$ for all $s \in S$. In this case $\psi$ is given by : $$ \psi(h, s) = \psi\bigl((h, 1_S)\cdot (1_H, s)\bigl) = (h, 1_S) \cdot \bigl(r(s), v(s)\bigl) = \bigl(h r(s), v(s)\bigl) $$ for all $h \in H$ and $s \in S$. Now, $\psi(1_H, 1_S) = (1_H, 1_{S'})$ if and only if $r$ and $v$ are unitary maps. Assuming this unitary condition, we can easily prove that $\psi$ is a morphism of groups if and only if the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:p1}) - (\ref{eq:p4}) hold for the pair $(r, v)$. It remains to be proved that $\psi$ given by (\ref{eq:p5}) is an isomorphism if and only if $v: S\to S'$ is a bijective map. Assume first that $\psi$ is an isomorphism. Then $v$ is surjective and for $s_{1}$, $s_{2} \in S$ such that $v(s_{1}) = v(s_{2})$ we have: $$ \psi(1_H, s_{2}) = \bigl(r(s_{2}), v(s_{2})\bigl) = \bigl(r(s_{2}), v(s_{1})\bigl) = \psi\bigl( r(s_{2}) r(s_{1})^{-1}, \, s_{1}\bigl) $$ Hence $s_{1} = s_{2}$ and $v$ is injective. Conversely is straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: A morphism stabilizing $H$ is determined by $\psi(1,s)=(r(s),v(s))$; unitality and the morphism property give (30)-(33), and injectivity of $v$ follows from that of $\psi$.

nodes.name: Equivalent group extending structures
nodes.statement: \delabel{equiv1} Two elements $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f)$ and $(\ast', \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ of ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S))$ are called \emph{equivalent} and we denote this by $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f) \sim (\ast', \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ if there exists a pair $(r, v)$ of unitary maps $r: S \rightarrow H$, $v: S \rightarrow S$ such that $v$ is a bijection on the set $S$ and the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:p1}) - (\ref{eq:p4}) are fulfilled.
nodes.statement_short: Two group extending structures on $S$ are equivalent if related by a unitary pair $(r,v)$ with $v$ bijective satisfying (30)-(33).
nodes.label: de:equiv1

nodes.name: Equivalence relation ~ on GES
nodes.statement: It follows from Proposition~\ref{pr:clasif1} that $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f) \sim (\ast', \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ if and only if there exists $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ an isomorphism of groups that stabilizes $H$. Thus, $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on the set ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S))$.
conclusions: $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on the set ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S))$

nodes.name: Classifying set K^2(H,(S,1_S))
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S))$ the quotient set ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S)) /\sim$.

nodes.name: Category C(H,(S,1_S))
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C} (H, (S, 1_S) )$ be the category whose class of objects is the set ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S))$. A morphism $\psi : (\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f) \to (\ast', \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ in $\mathcal{C} (H, (S, 1_S) )$ is a morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ that stabilizes $H$.

nodes.name: Argument for Theorem 2.16
nodes.statement: The main result of this paper which gives the full answer to the ES-problem now follows as a direct application of Proposition~\ref{pr:clasif1}: the classifying object for the ES-problem is ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S))$ constructed above.
nodes.statement_short: Direct application of Proposition 2.14.

nodes.name: Classification theorem for the ES-problem
nodes.statement: \thlabel{clasif1a} Let $H$ be a group and $(S, 1_S)$ a pointed set. Then there exists a bijection between the set of objects of the skeleton of the category $\mathcal{C} (H, (S, 1_S) )$ and ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S))$.
nodes.statement_short: Isomorphism classes (stabilizing $H$) of unified products on $(S,1_S)$ are in bijection with ${\mathcal K}^2_\ltimes(H,(S,1_S))$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a group and $(S, 1_S)$ a pointed set.
conclusions: there exists a bijection between the set of objects of the skeleton of the category $\mathcal{C} (H, (S, 1_S) )$ and ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S))$
nodes.label: th:clasif1a

nodes.name: Twisted tensor product algebras
nodes.statement: \relabel{pana} At the level of algebras the bicrossed product is known under the name of \emph{twisted tensor product algebra}. \cite[Theorem 4.4]{panaite} provides sufficient conditions for two bicrossed products of algebras $A\bowtie B$ and $A ' \bowtie B$ to be isomorphic such that the isomorphism stabilizes $B$. The result in \cite[Theorem 4.4]{panaite} can be improved and generalized in the spirit of Proposition~\ref{pr:clasif1}.

nodes.name: Morphisms stabilizing H and S
nodes.statement: \prlabel{clasif2} Let $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$, $\Omega ' (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_{S}, \ast'), \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f' \bigl)$ be two group extending structures of a group $H$. Then there exists a morphism $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ that stabilizes $H$ and $S$ if and only if $\triangleleft = \triangleleft'$ and there exists a unitary map $r: S \rightarrow H$ such that $\triangleright$, $\ast$ and $f$ are implemented by $\triangleright '$, $\ast'$ and $f'$ via $r$ as follows: \begin{eqnarray} s \triangleright h &=& r(s)\, \bigl(s \triangleright' h \bigl) \, r(s \triangleleft h)^{-1} \eqlabel{p2b} \\ s_{1} \ast s_{2} &=& \bigl( s_{1} \triangleleft r(s_{2})\bigl) \, \ast' \, s_{2} \eqlabel{p3b}\\ f(s_1, s_2) &=& r(s_{1}) \, \bigl( s_{1} \triangleright' r(s_{2}) \bigl) \, f' ( s_{1} \triangleleft r(s_{2}), \, s_2 ) \, r(s_{1} * s_{2})^{-1} \eqlabel{p4b} \end{eqnarray} for all $s$, $s_{1}$, $s_{2} \in S$ and $h \in H$. Furthermore, any morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes S \to H \ltimes' S$ that stabilizes $H$ and $S$ is an isomorphism of groups and is given by \begin{equation}\eqlabel{p5b} \psi(h, \, s) = \bigl(h \, r(s), \, s\bigl) \end{equation} for all $h \in H$, $s \in S$.
nodes.statement_short: A morphism stabilizing both $H$ and $S$ exists iff $\triangleleft=\triangleleft'$ and a unitary $r$ relates $\triangleright,\ast,f$ to $\triangleright',\ast',f'$; such morphisms are isomorphisms.
assumptions: be two group extending structures of a group $H$
conclusions: there exists a morphism $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S$ that stabilizes $H$ and $S$ if and only if $\triangleleft = \triangleleft'$ and there exists a unitary map $r: S \rightarrow H$
any morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes S \to H \ltimes' S$ that stabilizes $H$ and $S$ is an isomorphism of groups

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.18
nodes.statement: Indeed, using Proposition~\ref{pr:clasif1} any morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes S \to H \ltimes 'S$ that makes the left square of (\ref{eq:D2}) commutative is given by (\ref{eq:p5}) for some unique maps $(u, v)$. nodes.name: Cohomologous triples
nodes.statement: \delabel{equiv111} Let $H$ be a group, $(S, 1_S)$ a pointed set and $\triangleleft : S \times H \to S$ a right action of $H$ on $S$. Two elements $(\ast, \, \triangleright, \, f)$ and $(\ast', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ of ${\mathcal S} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S), \triangleleft)$ are called \emph{cohomologous} and we denote this by $(\ast, \, \triangleright, \, f) \approx (\ast', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ if there exists a unitary map $r: S \rightarrow H$ such that \begin{eqnarray*} s_{1} \ast s_{2} &=& \bigl( s_{1} \triangleleft r(s_{2})\bigl) \, \ast' \, s_{2} \eqlabel{p3b1}\\ s \triangleright h &=& r(s)\, \bigl(s \triangleright' h \bigl) \, r(s \triangleleft h)^{-1} \eqlabel{p2b1} \\ f(s_1, s_2) &=& r(s_{1}) \, \bigl( s_{1} \triangleright' r(s_{2}) \bigl) \, f' ( s_{1} \triangleleft r(s_{2}), \, s_2 ) \, r(s_{1} * s_{2})^{-1} \eqlabel{p4b1} \end{eqnarray*} for all $s$, $s_{1}$, $s_{2} \in S$ and $h \in H$.

nodes.name: The Schreier theorem for unified products
nodes.statement: \textbf{(The Schreier theorem for unified products)}\colabel{clasif2bb} Let $H$ be a group, $(S, 1_S)$ a pointed set and $\triangleleft$ a right action of $H$ on $S$. Then there exists a bijection between the set of objects of the skeleton of the category $\mathcal{D} (H, (S, 1_S), \triangleleft )$ and ${\mathcal H}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S), \triangleleft)$.

nodes.name: H^2 as counterpart of second cohomology group

nodes.name: Unified products isomorphic to crossed products
nodes.statement: \colabel{cazspec1} Let $H$ be a group, $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ a group extending structure of $H$ and $(H, G, \triangleright', f')$ a crossed system of groups. Then there exists $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H\#_{\triangleright'}^{f'} G$ an isomorphism of groups that stabilizes $H$ if and only if the right action $\triangleleft$ of $\Omega (H)$ is the trivial one and there exists a pair $(r, v)$, where $r: S \rightarrow H$ is a unitary map, $v: (S, \ast) \rightarrow G$ is an isomorphism of groups such that: \begin{eqnarray} s \triangleright h &=& r(s)\, \bigl(v(s) \triangleright' h \bigl) \, r(s)^{-1} \eqlabel{p2xx} \\ f(s_1, s_2) &=& r(s_{1}) \, \bigl( v(s_{1}) \triangleright' r(s_{2}) \bigl) \, f' \bigl( v(s_{1}), \, v(s_2) \bigl) \,\, r(s_{1} * s_{2})^{-1} \eqlabel{p4xx} \end{eqnarray} for all $s$, $s_{1}$, $s_{2} \in S$ and $h \in H$.
nodes.statement_short: $H\ltimes_\Omega S\cong H\#^{f'}_{\triangleright'}G$ stabilizing $H$ iff $\triangleleft$ is trivial and a unitary $r$ and group isomorphism $v$ satisfy (39)-(40).
assumptions: Let $H$ be a group, $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ a group extending structure of $H$ and $(H, G, \triangleright', f')$ a crossed system of groups.
conclusions: there exists $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H\#_{\triangleright'}^{f'} G$ an isomorphism of groups that stabilizes $H$ if and only if the right action $\triangleleft$ of $\Omega (H)$ is the trivial one

nodes.name: Unified products isomorphic to bicrossed products
nodes.statement: \colabel{cazspec2} Let $H$ be a group, $\Omega (H) = \bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ a group extending structure of $H$ and $(H, G, \triangleleft', \triangleright')$ a matched pair of groups. nodes.name: Computing K^2 is the remaining challenge
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{th:clasif1a} offers the theoretical answer to the ES-problem at the level of groups. The challenge that remains is a computational one: for a given group $H$ and a pointed set $(S, 1_S)$ we have to compute explicitly the cohomological object ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S))$: it classifies up to an isomorphism of groups that stabilizes $H$ all groups that contain $H$ as a subgroup of index $|S|$.

nodes.name: Set T(H) of pairs (h_0, D)
nodes.statement: For a group $H$ we shall denote by ${\mathcal T} (H) \subseteq H \times {\rm Aut} (H)$ the set consisting of all pairs $(h_0, \, D)$, where $h_0\in H$, $D : H \to H$ is an automorphism of $H$ such that for any $h\in H$: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ind2aa} D(h_0) = h_0, \qquad D^2 (h) = h_0 h h_0^{-1} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: ${\mathcal T}(H)$: pairs $(h_0,D)$ with $D\in\mathrm{Aut}(H)$, $D(h_0)=h_0$ and $D^2$ equal to conjugation by $h_0$.

nodes.name: Classification of groups containing H as a subgroup of index 2
nodes.statement: \prlabel{indice2} Let $H$ be a group and $S = \{1_S, \, c\}$ a set with two elements. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] There exists a bijection between the set ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S))$ of all group extending structures of $H$ and ${\mathcal T} (H)$. The bijection is given such that the group extending structure $\bigl( (S, 1_S, \ast), \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f \bigl)$ corresponding to $(h_0, \, D) \in {\mathcal T} (H)$ is defined as follows: $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action of $H$ on $S$, $\ast$ is given by $c \ast c = 1_S$, the left action $\triangleright : S \times H \to H$ and the cocycle $f: S \times S \to H$ are given for any $h\in H$ by: \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ind2} c \triangleright h := D(h), \qquad f(c, c) := h_0 \end{equation} \item[(2)] There exists a bijection ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S)) \cong {\mathcal T} (H)/ \sim $, where $\sim$ is the equivalence relation defined as follows: $(h_0, D) \sim (h'_0, D')$ if and only if there exists $g\in H$ such that for any $h\in H$ \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ind2bb} h_0 = g D' (g) \, h'_0, \qquad D(h) = g D'(h) g^{-1} \end{equation} The bijection between ${\mathcal T} (H)/ \sim $ and the isomorphism classes of all groups that contain and stabilize $H$ as a subgroup of index $2$ is given by $$ \overline{(h_0, \, D)} \mapsto H\ltimes_{(h_0, D)} S $$ where we denote by $H\ltimes_{(h_0, D)} S$ the unified product associated to the group extending structure constructed in (\ref{eq:ind2}) for a given $(h_0, D) \in {\mathcal T} (H)$ and $\overline{(h_0, \, D)}$ is the equivalence class of $(h_0, \, D)$ via the relation $\sim$. Explicitly, the multiplication on the group $H\ltimes_{(h_0, D)} S$ is given for any $h$, $h_{1}$, $h_2 \in H$ by: \begin{eqnarray*} (h_{1}, 1_{S}) \cdot (h_{2}, 1_{S}) &=& (h_{1} h_{2}, 1_{S}), \qquad (1, c) \cdot (1, c) = (h_{0}, 1_{S}) \\ (h, 1_{S}) \cdot (1, c) &=& (h, c), \qquad \quad \,\, (1, c) \cdot (h, 1_{S}) = (D(h), c) \end{eqnarray*} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $|S|=2$, group extending structures correspond to ${\mathcal T}(H)$ and ${\mathcal K}^2_\ltimes(H,(S,1_S))\cong{\mathcal T}(H)/\sim$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a group and $S = \{1_S, \, c\}$ a set with two elements.
conclusions: There exists a bijection between the set ${\mathcal G} {\mathcal E} {\mathcal S}$$(H, (S, 1_S))$ of all group extending structures of $H$ and ${\mathcal T} (H)$.
There exists a bijection ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S)) \cong {\mathcal T} (H)/ \sim $
nodes.label: pr:indice2

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.23
nodes.statement: $(1)$ We have to compute the set of all maps $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f)$ satisfying the normalizing conditions (\ref{eq:ES3}), (\ref{eq:nor1a}) as well as the compatibility conditions $(ES1)$-$(ES7)$. First we prove that $c \triangleleft h = c$, for all $h\in H$, i.e. $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action and $c \ast c = 1_S$, i.e. $S = C_2$, the cyclic group of order $2$. Indeed, using (\ref{eq:nor1a}) we already know that $1_S \triangleleft h = 1_S$, for all $h \in H$. Let $f : H \to S$ be a map such that $ c \triangleleft h = f(h)$, for all $h \in H$. Then, $f$ is a unit preserving map since (\ref{eq:nor1a}) holds. We will prove that $f (h) = c$, for all $h \in H$, and hence $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action. Indeed, $(ES1)$ tells us that $\triangleleft$ is a right action: the condition $c \triangleleft (g h) = (c \triangleleft g) \triangleleft h$ takes the form $f (g h) = f(g) \triangleleft h$, for all $g$, $h \in H$. Assume, that there exists $g \in H$ such that $f (g) = 1_S$. Then we obtain that $f (g h) = 1_S \triangleleft h = 1_S$, i.e. $f (gh) = 1_S$, for all $h\in H$. Thus, $f$ is the trivial map, that is $c \triangleleft h = 1_S$, for all $h \in H$. Then, axiom $(ES2)$ applied for $s_1 = s_2 = s_3 = c$ implies that $ (c \ast c) \ast c = c \ast c$ and using $(ES7)$ we obtain $c = 1_S$, which is a contradiction. Thus, $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action; it follows from $(ES1)$ that $\ast$ is a group structure on $S$ i.e. $c \ast c = 1_S$. Now, any normalizing map $ \triangleright : S \times H \to H$ is uniquely implemented by a map $D : H \to H$ such that $c \triangleright h = D(h)$, for all $h\in H$, and any normalized map $f : S \times S \to H$ is uniquely determined by an element $h_0 \in H$ such that $f (c, c) = h_0$. Now we can easily see that the compatibility conditions $(ES1)$, $(ES2)$, $(ES4)$ are trivially fulfilled, while $(ES3)$ is equivalent to the fact that $D$ is an endomorphism of $H$, axiom $(ES5)$ takes the equivalent form given by the right hand side of (\ref{eq:ind2aa}) while $(ES6)$ is the left hand side of (\ref{eq:ind2aa}). $(2)$ Let $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f)$ and $(\ast', \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ be two group extending structures associated to $(h_0, D)$ and $(h'_0, D') \in {\mathcal T} (H)$. Then, $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f) \sim (\ast', \triangleleft', \, \triangleright', \, f')$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{de:equiv1} if there exists a pair $(r, v)$ of unitary maps $r: S \rightarrow H$, $v: S \rightarrow S$ such that $v$ is a bijection on the set $S$ and the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:p1}) - (\ref{eq:p4}) are fulfilled. Since $|S| = 2$ and $v$ is a unitary bijection we obtain that $v$ is the identity map on $S$. On the other hand, the unitary map $r: S \to H$ is given by an element $g \in H$ such that $r (c) = g$. Taking into account the construction of the group extending structures from (\ref{eq:ind2}) we can easily show that the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:p1}) - (\ref{eq:p4}) take the equivalent form (\ref{eq:ind2bb}).
nodes.statement_short: Show by contradiction that $\triangleleft$ is trivial and $S=C_2$, then translate (ES3)-(ES6) into conditions on $(h_0,D)$. For (2), $v$ must be the identity and $r$ is one element $g$, turning (30)-(33) into (46).

nodes.name: Index-2 extensions for groups without outer automorphisms and abelian groups
nodes.statement: \exlabel{faraout} 1. Let $H$ be a group which has no outer automorphisms. The typical example is $S_n$, for $n \neq 6$. Then, in this case ${\mathcal T} (H)$ identifies with the set of all pairs $(h_0, a) \in H \times H$ such that : \begin{equation}\eqlabel{ind2aabb} a h_0 = h_0 a, \qquad a^2 h a^{-2} = h_0 h h_0^{-1} \end{equation} for all $h\in H$. Moreover, ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} (H, (S, 1_S)) \simeq {\mathcal T} (H)/ \sim $, where $(h_0, a) \sim (h'_0, a')$ if and only if there exists $g\in H$ such that $h_0 = g a' g a'^{-1} h'_0$ and $a h a^{-1} = g a' h a'^{-1} g^{-1}$, for all $h\in H$. 2. Let $H$ be an abelian group. Then ${\mathcal T} (H)$ is the set of all pairs $(h_0, \, D) \in H \times {\rm Aut} (H)$, such that $D^2 = {\rm Id}_H$ and $D (h_0) = h_0$. Two such pairs $(h_0, D)$ and $(h'_0, D')$ are equivalent if and only if $D = D'$ and there exists $g\in H$ such that $h_0 = g D'(g) h'_0$. In particular, if $H = {\mathbb Z}$ we obtain that ${\mathcal K}^{2}_{\ltimes} ({\mathbb Z}, (S, 1_S)) \cong \{ \overline{(0, \, {\rm Id}_{{\mathbb Z}})}, \, \overline{(0, \, - {\rm Id}_{{\mathbb Z}})}, \, \overline{(1, \, {\rm Id}_{{\mathbb Z}})} \}$. Thus, up to an isomorphism of groups that stabilizes ${\mathbb Z}$ there are three groups that contain ${\mathbb Z}$ as a subgroup of index $2$: the direct product ${\mathbb Z} \times C_2$ corresponding to $\overline{(0, \, {\rm Id}_{{\mathbb Z}})}$, the semidirect product ${\mathbb Z} \ltimes C_2$ corresponding to $\overline{(0, \, - {\rm Id}_{{\mathbb Z}})}$ and the crossed product ${\mathbb Z} \#^f C_2$ associated to the non-trivial cocycle coressponding to $\overline{(1, \, {\rm Id}_{{\mathbb Z}})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Specializes Proposition 2.23 to groups without outer automorphisms and to abelian groups; for $\mathbb{Z}$ there are exactly three groups.
nodes.label: ex:faraout

nodes.name: G-equivariant and fiber transitive principal bundle
nodes.statement: The $H$-principal bundle $(E, S, \pi)$ \cite{KN} is said to be (right) $G$-equivariant if there are differentiable right actions of $G$ on $E$ and $S$ such that $\pi$ is $G$-equivariant and the left action of $H$ and the right action of $G$ on $E$ commute; we say that the $G$-action is fiber transitive if the action of $G$ on $S$ is transitive.
nodes.statement_short: Right $G$-actions on $E$ and $S$ making $\pi$ equivariant and commuting with $H$; fiber transitive if $G$ is transitive on $S$.

nodes.name: Hidden symmetries problem for principal bundles
nodes.statement: \textit{Let $K$ be a Lie group and let $(E, S, \pi)$ be an $K$-equivariant $H$-principal bundle. Does there exist a Lie group $G\supset K$ endowed with actions on $E$ and $S$ that extend the corresponding $K$-actions such that $(E, S, \pi)$ becomes $G$-equivariant fiber transitive?}
nodes.statement_short: Can the $K$-action on a $K$-equivariant $H$-principal bundle be extended to a fiber transitive action of a larger Lie group $G\supset K$?

nodes.name: Hidden symmetries
nodes.statement: If such a $G$ exists we say that the bundle $(E, S, \pi)$ has \textit{hidden symmetries}.

nodes.name: Unified products give hidden symmetries of trivial bundles
nodes.statement: The unified product associated to an extending structure provides an answer to the above question for $E = H \times S$ (the trivial $H$-bundle over $S$), $K=H$, and the actions on $S$ and $E$ given respectively by $h\cdot k:=s\triangleleft k$ and $(h, s)\cdot k:= (h(s\triangleright k), s\triangleleft k)$, for all $h\in H$, $s\in S$, $k\in K$. If the right action of $H$ on $S$ has a fixed point $1_{S}$, and $S$ has an $H$-group structure then the bundle becomes $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S)$-equivariant fiber transitive. Therefore, the existence of $H$-group structures on $S$ is related to the existence of hidden symmetries.
assumptions: If the right action of $H$ on $S$ has a fixed point $1_{S}$, and $S$ has an $H$-group structure
conclusions: the bundle becomes $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S)$-equivariant fiber transitive

nodes.name: Construct p
nodes.statement: (1) Using the axiom of choice we can fix $ \Gamma = (x_i)_{i\in I} \subset E $ to be a system of representatives for the right congruence modulo $H$ in $E$ such that $1 \in \Gamma$. Then for any $x\in E$ there exists an unique $h_x \in H$ and an unique $x_{i_0} \in \Gamma$ such that $x = h_x \, x_{i_0}$. Thus, there exists a well defined map $p : E \to H$ given by the formula $p (x) := h_x$, for all $x\in E$. As $1 \in \Gamma$ we have that $ p (1) = 1$. Moreover, for any $h\in H$ and $x\in E$ we have that $h x = h h_x \, x_{i_0}$. Thus $p (h x) = h h_x = h p(x)$, as needed.
nodes.section: 2 Group extending structures and unified products
nodes.statement_short: Define $p$ via a system of right coset representatives containing 1.

nodes.name: phi is bijective
nodes.statement: (2) We note that $p (x)^{-1} x \in S$ as $ p \bigl( p (x)^{-1} \, x \bigl) = p (x)^{-1} p(x) = 1 $, for all $x\in E$. The rest is straightforward.
nodes.section: 2 Group extending structures and unified products
nodes.statement_short: Check $p(x)^{-1}x\in S$, giving the inverse of $\varphi$.

nodes.name: Transported multiplication
nodes.statement: (3) First we note that $\triangleleft$ and $\ast$ are well defined maps. Next, we can easily prove that the following two formulas hold: \begin{eqnarray} p(s_1 h_2 s_2) &=& (s_1 \triangleright h_2) f (s_1 \triangleleft h_2 , s_2) \eqlabel{inmaa} \\ (s_1 \triangleleft h_2) \ast s_2 &=& p (s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2 \eqlabel{inmab} \end{eqnarray} for all $s_1$, $s_2\in S$ and $h_2 \in H$. Indeed, \begin{eqnarray*} (s_1 \triangleright h_2) f (s_1 \triangleleft h_2 , s_2) &{=}& p(s_1 h_2) \, p\bigl( (s_1 \triangleleft h_2) s_2 \bigl)\\ &{=}& p(s_1 h_2) \, p \bigl( p(s_1 h_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2 \bigl)\\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:33ab})} {=}& p (s_1 h_2 s_2) \end{eqnarray*} Similarly, we can prove that (\ref{eq:inmab}) holds. Now, $\varphi : H \times S \to E$ is a bijection between the set $H \times S$ and the group $E$. Thus, there exists a unique group structure $\cdot$ on the set $H \times S$ such that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of groups. This group structure is obtained by transferring the group structure from $E$ via the bijection $\varphi$, i.e. is given by: \begin{eqnarray*} (h_{1}, s_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, s_{2}) &{=}& \varphi^{-1} \bigl( \varphi (h_1, s_1) \varphi (h_2, s_2) \bigl) \,\, = \varphi^{-1} (h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2)\\ &{=}& \bigl( p(h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2), \, p(h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2 \bigl)\\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:33ab})} {=}& \bigl( h_1 p(s_1 h_2 s_2), \, p(s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2\bigl) \\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:inmaa}), (\ref{eq:inmab})} {=}& \Bigl( \, h_{1} (s_{1} \triangleright h_{2}) f(s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}, \, s_{2}), \,\, (s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}) \ast s_{2} \Bigl ) \end{eqnarray*} for all $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2\in S$ as needed.

nodes.statement_short: Compute the group structure transported from $E$ along $\varphi$.

nodes.statement: First we note that $\triangleleft$ and $\ast$ are well defined maps. Next, we can easily prove that the following two formulas hold: \begin{eqnarray} p(s_1 h_2 s_2) &=& (s_1 \triangleright h_2) f (s_1 \triangleleft h_2 , s_2) \eqlabel{inmaa} \\ (s_1 \triangleleft h_2) \ast s_2 &=& p (s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2 \eqlabel{inmab} \end{eqnarray} for all $s_1$, $s_2\in S$ and $h_2 \in H$.

nodes.name: Verify auxiliary formulas
nodes.statement: Indeed, \begin{eqnarray*} (s_1 \triangleright h_2) f (s_1 \triangleleft h_2 , s_2) &{=}& p(s_1 h_2) \, p\bigl( (s_1 \triangleleft h_2) s_2 \bigl)\\ &{=}& p(s_1 h_2) \, p \bigl( p(s_1 h_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2 \bigl)\\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:33ab})} {=}& p (s_1 h_2 s_2) \end{eqnarray*} Similarly, we can prove that (\ref{eq:inmab}) holds.

nodes.name: Transport the structure
nodes.statement: Now, $\varphi : H \times S \to E$ is a bijection between the set $H \times S$ and the group $E$. Thus, there exists a unique group structure $\cdot$ on the set $H \times S$ such that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of groups. This group structure is obtained by transferring the group structure from $E$ via the bijection $\varphi$, i.e. is given by: \begin{eqnarray*} (h_{1}, s_{1}) \cdot (h_{2}, s_{2}) &{=}& \varphi^{-1} \bigl( \varphi (h_1, s_1) \varphi (h_2, s_2) \bigl) \,\, = \varphi^{-1} (h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2)\\ &{=}& \bigl( p(h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2), \, p(h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} h_1 s_1 h_2 s_2 \bigl)\\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:33ab})} {=}& \bigl( h_1 p(s_1 h_2 s_2), \, p(s_1 h_2 s_2)^{-1} s_1 h_2 s_2\bigl) \\ &\stackrel{(\ref{eq:inmaa}), (\ref{eq:inmab})} {=}& \Bigl( \, h_{1} (s_{1} \triangleright h_{2}) f(s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}, \, s_{2}), \,\, (s_{1} \triangleleft h_{2}) \ast s_{2} \Bigl ) \end{eqnarray*} for all $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2\in S$ as needed.
nodes.section: 2 Group extending structures and unified products
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the multiplication of $E$ via $\varphi$ and simplify with (11), (14), (15).

nodes.name: Unit and plan
nodes.statement: We know that $(1_{H}, 1_{S})$ is a unit for the operation defined by (\ref{eq:13a}). We prove now that $\cdot$ given by (\ref{eq:13a}) is associative if and only if the compatibility conditions $(ES1) - (ES6)$ hold.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to: associativity iff (ES1)-(ES6).

nodes.name: Associativity implies (ES1)-(ES6)
nodes.statement: Assume first that $\cdot$ is associative and let $h$, $h_{1}$, $h_{2} \in H$ and $s$, $s_1$, $s_{2} \in S$. The associativity condition $$ [(1_H, s)\cdot (h_{1}, 1_S)]\cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (1_H, s)\cdot [(h_{1}, 1_S)\cdot (h_2, 1_S)] $$ gives, after we use the cross relations (\ref{eq:15}) and (\ref{eq:13}), $ (s \triangleright h_1, \, s\triangleleft h_1 ) \cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (1_H, s) \cdot (h_1 h_2, \, 1_S)$. Thus $ \Bigl((s \triangleright h_{1}) \bigl( (s \triangleleft h_{1}) \triangleright h_{2} \bigl), \, (s\triangleleft h_1) \triangleleft h_2 \Bigl) = \bigl(s \triangleright (h_1 h_2), \, s \triangleleft (h_1 h_2) \bigl)$ and hence $(ES1)$ and $(ES3)$ hold. Now, by writing the associativity condition $[(1_H, s_1)\cdot (1_H, s_2)]\cdot (1_H, s_3) = (1_H, s_1)\cdot [(1_H, s_2)\cdot (1_H, s_3)]$ and computing this equality using the cross relation (\ref{eq:14}) it follows that the compatibility conditions $(ES2)$ and $(ES6)$ hold. Finally, if we write the associativity condition $[(1_H, s_1)\cdot (1_H, s_2)]\cdot (h, 1_S) = (1_H, s_1)\cdot [(1_H, s_2)\cdot (h, 1_S)]$ and use (\ref{eq:14}) and then (\ref{eq:15}) we obtain that $(ES4)$ and $(ES5)$ hold.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Test associativity on triples of generators.

nodes.name: Get (ES1),(ES3)
nodes.statement: Assume first that $\cdot$ is associative and let $h$, $h_{1}$, $h_{2} \in H$ and $s$, $s_1$, $s_{2} \in S$. The associativity condition $$ [(1_H, s)\cdot (h_{1}, 1_S)]\cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (1_H, s)\cdot [(h_{1}, 1_S)\cdot (h_2, 1_S)] $$ gives, after we use the cross relations (\ref{eq:15}) and (\ref{eq:13}), $ (s \triangleright h_1, \, s\triangleleft h_1 ) \cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (1_H, s) \cdot (h_1 h_2, \, 1_S)$. Thus $ \Bigl((s \triangleright h_{1}) \bigl( (s \triangleleft h_{1}) \triangleright h_{2} \bigl), \, (s\triangleleft h_1) \triangleleft h_2 \Bigl) = \bigl(s \triangleright (h_1 h_2), \, s \triangleleft (h_1 h_2) \bigl)$ and hence $(ES1)$ and $(ES3)$ hold.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Associativity on $(1_H,s),(h_1,1_S),(h_2,1_S)$ yields (ES1), (ES3).

nodes.name: Get (ES2),(ES6)
nodes.statement: Now, by writing the associativity condition $[(1_H, s_1)\cdot (1_H, s_2)]\cdot (1_H, s_3) = (1_H, s_1)\cdot [(1_H, s_2)\cdot (1_H, s_3)]$ and computing this equality using the cross relation (\ref{eq:14}) it follows that the compatibility conditions $(ES2)$ and $(ES6)$ hold.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Associativity on three elements $(1_H,s_i)$ yields (ES2), (ES6).

nodes.name: Get (ES4),(ES5)
nodes.statement: Finally, if we write the associativity condition $[(1_H, s_1)\cdot (1_H, s_2)]\cdot (h, 1_S) = (1_H, s_1)\cdot [(1_H, s_2)\cdot (h, 1_S)]$ and use (\ref{eq:14}) and then (\ref{eq:15}) we obtain that $(ES4)$ and $(ES5)$ hold.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Associativity on $(1_H,s_1),(1_H,s_2),(h,1_S)$ yields (ES4), (ES5).

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that the compatibility conditions $(ES1) - (ES6)$ hold. Then, by a rather long but straightforward computation, which can be provided upon request, we can prove that the operation $\cdot$ is associative, that is $(h_{1}, s_{1})\cdot [(h_{2}, s_{2}) \cdot (h_{3}, s_{3})] = [(h_{1}, s_{1})\cdot (h_{2}, s_{2})]\cdot (h_{3}, s_{3})$, for all $h_1$, $h_2$, $h_{3} \in H$ and $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_{3} \in S$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: (ES1)-(ES6) imply associativity by a long direct computation.

nodes.name: Monoid characterization
nodes.statement: To conclude, we have proved that $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is a monoid if and only if $(ES1) - (ES6)$ hold.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Combine both directions: monoid iff (ES1)-(ES6).

nodes.name: Reduce to invertibility
nodes.statement: Assume now that $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is a monoid: it remains to be proved that the monoid is actually a group if and only if $(ES7)$ holds.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Remains: the monoid is a group iff (ES7).

nodes.name: Elements (h,1_S) invertible
nodes.statement: Indeed, in the monoid $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ we have: $$ (h, 1_S)\cdot (1_H, s) = (h, s), \qquad (h_1, 1_S) \cdot (h_2, 1_S) = (h_1 h_2, 1_S) $$ for all $h$, $h_1$, $h_2 \in H$ and $s\in S$. In particular, any element of the form $(h, 1_S)$, for $h\in H$ is invertible in $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Elements $(h,1_S)$ are invertible.

nodes.name: Reduce to left inverses of (1_H,s)
nodes.statement: Now, a monoid is a group if and only if each of his elements has a left inverse. As $\cdot$ is associative it follows from: $$ (h^{-1}, 1_S)\cdot (h, s) = (1_H, s) $$ that $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is a group if and only if $(1_H, s)$ has a left inverse for all $s\in S$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: A monoid is a group iff left inverses exist; reduce to elements $(1_H,s)$.

nodes.name: Left inverse iff (ES7)
nodes.statement: Hence, for any $s\in S$ there exist elements $s' \in S$ and $h'\in H$ such that $$ (h' , s' ) \cdot (1_H, s) = \bigl ( h' f (s', s), \, s' \ast s\bigl ) = (1_H, 1_S) $$ This is of course equivalent to the fact that $s' \ast s = 1_S$ for all $s \in S$ and $h' = f\bigl( s', \, s \bigl)^{-1}$. The proof is now finished.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: A left inverse of $(1_H,s)$ exists iff $s'\ast s=1_S$, i.e. (ES7).

nodes.name: Inverse formula
nodes.statement: We note that the inverse of an element $(h, s)$ in the group $( H \ltimes S , \cdot )$ is given by the formula $$ (h, \, s)^{-1} = \bigl( f(s', \, s)^{-1} (s' \triangleright h^{-1}), \, s' \triangleleft h^{-1}\bigl) $$ where $s' \ast s = 1_S$.
nodes.section: The abstract construction of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Explicit formula for the inverse of $(h,s)$.

nodes.name: Initial object
nodes.statement: $(1)$ It is easy to see that $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S, (i_H, i_S))$ is an object in the category ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$. Let $(G, (u,v))$ be an object in ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$. We need to prove that there exists an unique morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \rightarrow G$ such that the following diagram commutes: $$ \xymatrix{ H\ar[r]^{i_{H}}\ar[dr]_{u} & H \ltimes_{\Omega} S\ar[d]^{\psi} & S\ar[l]_{i_{S}}\ar[dl]^{v} \\ &G } $$ Assume first that $\psi$ satisfies the above condition. We obtain: $\psi ((h,s)) = \psi((h, 1_S) \cdot(1_H, s)) = \psi ((h, 1_S)) \psi((1_H, s)) = (\psi \circ i_H)(h) (\psi \circ i_S)(s)) = u(h)v(s)$, for all $h \in H$, $s \in S$ and we proved that $\psi$ is uniquely determined by $u$ and $v$. The existence of $\psi$ can be proved as follows: we define $\psi: H\ltimes_{\Omega} S \rightarrow G$ by $\psi ((h, s)) := u(h)v(s)$, for all $h\in H$ and $s\in S$. The fact that $\psi$ is a morphism of groups is just a straightforward computation and the commutativity of the diagram is obvious.
nodes.section: The universal properties of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Show the unified product is initial in ${}_{\Omega(H)}\mathcal{C}$.

nodes.name: Set up universal problem
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that $(H \ltimes_{\Omega} S, (i_H, i_S))$ is an object in the category ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$. Let $(G, (u,v))$ be an object in ${}_{\Omega (H)}{\mathcal C}$. We need to prove that there exists an unique morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \rightarrow G$ such that the following diagram commutes: $$ \xymatrix{ H\ar[r]^{i_{H}}\ar[dr]_{u} & H \ltimes_{\Omega} S\ar[d]^{\psi} & S\ar[l]_{i_{S}}\ar[dl]^{v} \\ &G } $$
nodes.section: The universal properties of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: It is an object; need a unique $\psi$ making the diagram commute.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of psi
nodes.statement: Assume first that $\psi$ satisfies the above condition. We obtain: $\psi ((h,s)) = \psi((h, 1_S) \cdot(1_H, s)) = \psi ((h, 1_S)) \psi((1_H, s)) = (\psi \circ i_H)(h) (\psi \circ i_S)(s)) = u(h)v(s)$, for all $h \in H$, $s \in S$ and we proved that $\psi$ is uniquely determined by $u$ and $v$.
nodes.section: The universal properties of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Any such $\psi$ equals $u(h)v(s)$.

nodes.name: Existence of psi
nodes.statement: The existence of $\psi$ can be proved as follows: we define $\psi: H\ltimes_{\Omega} S \rightarrow G$ by $\psi ((h, s)) := u(h)v(s)$, for all $h\in H$ and $s\in S$. The fact that $\psi$ is a morphism of groups is just a straightforward computation and the commutativity of the diagram is obvious.
nodes.section: The universal properties of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi(h,s)=u(h)v(s)$; it is a group morphism.

nodes.name: Final object
nodes.statement: $(2)$ Similar to $(1)$.
nodes.section: The universal properties of the unified product
nodes.statement_short: Dual argument for $\mathcal{D}_{\Omega(H)}$.

nodes.name: psi determined by (r, v)
nodes.statement: A morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes_{\Omega} S \to H \ltimes_{\Omega'} S'$ that makes the left square of the diagram (\ref{eq:D2}) commutative is uniquely determined by two maps $r = r_{\psi}: S \rightarrow H$, $v = v_{\psi}: S \rightarrow S'$ such that $\psi(1, s) = \bigl( r(s), v(s)\bigl)$ for all $s \in S$. In this case $\psi$ is given by : $$ \psi(h, s) = \psi\bigl((h, 1_S)\cdot (1_H, s)\bigl) = (h, 1_S) \cdot \bigl(r(s), v(s)\bigl) = \bigl(h r(s), v(s)\bigl) $$ for all $h \in H$ and $s \in S$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\psi(1,s)=(r(s),v(s))$, so $\psi(h,s)=(hr(s),v(s))$.

nodes.name: Morphism conditions
nodes.statement: Now, $\psi(1_H, 1_S) = (1_H, 1_{S'})$ if and only if $r$ and $v$ are unitary maps. Assuming this unitary condition, we can easily prove that $\psi$ is a morphism of groups if and only if the compatibility conditions (\ref{eq:p1}) - (\ref{eq:p4}) hold for the pair $(r, v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Unitality of $\psi$ iff $r,v$ unitary; morphism iff (30)-(33).

nodes.name: Remaining claim
nodes.statement: It remains to be proved that $\psi$ given by (\ref{eq:p5}) is an isomorphism if and only if $v: S\to S'$ is a bijective map.
nodes.statement_short: Remains: $\psi$ iso iff $v$ bijective.

nodes.name: Isomorphism iff v bijective
nodes.statement: Assume first that $\psi$ is an isomorphism. Then $v$ is surjective and for $s_{1}$, $s_{2} \in S$ such that $v(s_{1}) = v(s_{2})$ we have: $$ \psi(1_H, s_{2}) = \bigl(r(s_{2}), v(s_{2})\bigl) = \bigl(r(s_{2}), v(s_{1})\bigl) = \psi\bigl( r(s_{2}) r(s_{1})^{-1}, \, s_{1}\bigl) $$ Hence $s_{1} = s_{2}$ and $v$ is injective. Conversely is straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: If $\psi$ is iso then $v$ is surjective and injective; converse straightforward.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2.14
nodes.statement: Indeed, using Proposition~\ref{pr:clasif1} any morphism of groups $\psi : H \ltimes S \to H \ltimes 'S$ that makes the left square of (\ref{eq:D2}) commutative is given by (\ref{eq:p5}) for some unique maps $(u, v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Morphisms stabilizing $H$ have the form (34).

nodes.name: Stabilizing S forces v = Id
nodes.statement: Now, such a morphism $\psi = \psi_{u, v}$ makes the right square of (\ref{eq:D2}) commutative if and only if $v$ is the identity map on $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Right square commutes iff $v=\mathrm{Id}_S$.

nodes.name: Specialize conditions
nodes.statement: Now the proof follows from Proposition~\ref{pr:clasif1}: (\ref{eq:p1}) implies that the right actions $\triangleleft$ and $\triangleleft'$ should be equal while $(\ref{eq:p2b})- (\ref{eq:p4b})$ are exactly $(\ref{eq:p2})- (\ref{eq:p4})$ for $v = {\rm Id}_S$ and $\triangleleft = \triangleleft'$.
nodes.statement_short: (30) forces $\triangleleft=\triangleleft'$ and (31)-(33) become (35)-(37).

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: $(1)$ We have to compute the set of all maps $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f)$ satisfying the normalizing conditions (\ref{eq:ES3}), (\ref{eq:nor1a}) as well as the compatibility conditions $(ES1)$-$(ES7)$. First we prove that $c \triangleleft h = c$, for all $h\in H$, i.e. $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action and $c \ast c = 1_S$, i.e. $S = C_2$, the cyclic group of order $2$. Indeed, using (\ref{eq:nor1a}) we already know that $1_S \triangleleft h = 1_S$, for all $h \in H$. Let $f : H \to S$ be a map such that $ c \triangleleft h = f(h)$, for all $h \in H$. Then, $f$ is a unit preserving map since (\ref{eq:nor1a}) holds. We will prove that $f (h) = c$, for all $h \in H$, and hence $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action. Indeed, $(ES1)$ tells us that $\triangleleft$ is a right action: the condition $c \triangleleft (g h) = (c \triangleleft g) \triangleleft h$ takes the form $f (g h) = f(g) \triangleleft h$, for all $g$, $h \in H$. Assume, that there exists $g \in H$ such that $f (g) = 1_S$. Then we obtain that $f (g h) = 1_S \triangleleft h = 1_S$, i.e. $f (gh) = 1_S$, for all $h\in H$. Thus, $f$ is the trivial map, that is $c \triangleleft h = 1_S$, for all $h \in H$. Then, axiom $(ES2)$ applied for $s_1 = s_2 = s_3 = c$ implies that $ (c \ast c) \ast c = c \ast c$ and using $(ES7)$ we obtain $c = 1_S$, which is a contradiction. Thus, $\triangleleft$ is the trivial action; it follows from $(ES1)$ that $\ast$ is a group structure on $S$ i.e. $c \ast c = 1_S$. Now, any normalizing map $ \triangleright : S \times H \to H$ is uniquely implemented by a map $D : H \to H$ such that $c \triangleright h = D(h)$, for all $h\in H$, and any normalized map $f : S \times S \to H$ is uniquely determined by an element $h_0 \in H$ such that $f (c, c) = h_0$. Now we can easily see that the compatibility conditions $(ES1)$, $(ES2)$, $(ES4)$ are trivially fulfilled, while $(ES3)$ is equivalent to the fact that $D$ is an endomorphism of $H$, axiom $(ES5)$ takes the equivalent form given by the right hand side of (\ref{eq:ind2aa}) while $(ES6)$ is the left hand side of (\ref{eq:ind2aa}).
nodes.statement_short: Determine all group extending structures on a two-element set.

nodes.name: Task
nodes.statement: We have to compute the set of all maps $(\ast, \triangleleft, \, \triangleright, \, f)$ satisfying the normalizing conditions (\ref{eq:ES3}), (\ref{eq:nor1a}) as well as the compatibility conditions $(ES1)$-$(ES7)$.
nodes.statement_short: Find all normalized maps satisfying (ES1)-(ES7).
